analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal grant fund to pay for free lawyers for low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since introduction, with 11 Democratic cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill sets up an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund and authorizes $100 million a year for five years (fiscal 2026 through 2030). States, local governments, and tribal governments get grants if they pass laws guaranteeing a free lawyer to tenants earning up to 200% of the federal poverty line who are facing eviction or loss of a housing subsidy. Federal money can also cover training and recruiting the attorneys who do this work, and the housing secretary is told to give extra priority to places with eviction-diversion programs, longer notice periods, and emergency rental assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants facing eviction get a lawyer at no cost, at a stage where studies and courthouse experience show representation sharply changes outcomes — tenants with counsel are far more likely to stay in their homes or negotiate a managed exit instead of a judgment that follows them into future housing applications. Cities and states that want to run such programs get federal money to help pay for it.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund with $100 million authorized for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030 to fund grants.

Grants go to states, local governments, and tribal governments that have enacted legislation guaranteeing free full legal representation to tenants at or below 200% of the federal poverty line in eviction cases and subsidy-termination cases.

The housing secretary must give priority to jurisdictions with just-cause eviction limits, at least 30 days' written notice, eviction diversion programs, or emergency rental assistance, and to applicants who will use funds to train and recruit eviction-defense attorneys.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers foot the $100 million a year. Landlords and property owners bear the practical cost: represented tenants contest cases more effectively, which means more disputes go to hearing, more negotiated settlements, and fewer quick default judgments in their favor.

drawbacks.text: The funding is modest relative to the problem: $100 million a year nationwide cannot cover counsel for all eligible tenants in high-eviction cities, so many jurisdictions would get only partial support even after committing to a universal right.

The bill changes no federal eviction law itself; it only pays governments that already pass their own right-to-counsel statutes, so coverage depends entirely on state and local legislatures choosing to act.

Opponents of eviction right-to-counsel laws generally argue they raise litigation costs and slow court cases for landlords, which can discourage small property owners — a cost the bill's text does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tenants it covers, the benefit is direct and substantial — eviction cases are fast, most tenants appear alone, and unrepresented tenants lose at high rates. The cost side is real but comparatively small: $100 million a year is a rounding error in the federal budget, and the main honest criticism is that it is too small to fulfill its own promise everywhere. The bigger limit is structural: the money only flows where local governments first pass their own laws, so the bill's reach depends on action it cannot compel.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 25, 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings or vote; the Congress is still in session, so it technically remains alive but has not moved.

narrative.text: Rep. Summer Lee introduced the bill in the House on July 25, 2025 with seven original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action is recorded.
Eleven House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been forced to lose anything, but the practical effect of inaction is that tenants continue to face eviction without lawyers and no federal money has moved to help.

for.name: Rep. Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Eviction Right to Counsel Act of 2025 in the House and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 11 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors are listed.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred on July 25, 2025 — no markup, hearing, or floor schedule recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors are House Democrats, and the bill sits with the Republican-run Judiciary Committee, which has not acted on it.

industries.note: Right-to-counsel laws mean tenants show up with lawyers, contest grounds for eviction, and settle on better terms, so landlords face slower cases and fewer automatic judgments. Many landlords also benefit when tenants get help negotiating exits instead of being removed without a hearing, so the hit is concentrated in cases they would otherwise win by default.

The fund pays for representation, attorney training, and recruitment, expanding funded work for eviction-defense lawyers. This is the delivery mechanism for the tenant benefit, not a handoff that redirects it.

analysis.trajectory: With a single Democratic sponsor, 11 cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action more than mid-2025 into the Congress, the realistic path is that the bill stays in the House Judiciary Committee and expires at the end of this Congress without a vote, the usual fate for a first-term bill from the minority party on a committee chaired by the opposition.
